## What is a Feature?
.pull-left[
- A Thing, or an Object in the real world

- Examples of Features: 

 - A Tree or a Lamp-post
 - A forest stand  
 - A city with building, streets, and parks  
 - A County or State
 - A Country 
 - An Island

]

.pull-right[

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.height="450px", out.width="900px"}

p1 <- ggplot() + 
  geom_fontawesome("fa-tree", color='green', size = 24) + theme_void()
p2 <- ggplot() + 
  geom_fontawesome("fa-ambulance", color='red', size = 24) + theme_void()
p3 <- ggplot() + 
  geom_fontawesome("fa-institution", color='grey', size = 24) + theme_void()
p4 <- ggplot() + 
  geom_fontawesome("fa-mortar-board", color='black', size = 24) + theme_void()
wrap_plots(list(p1,p2,p3,p4))

```

]
---

## What is a Feature Geometry?
.pull-left[
Features have a **geometry** describing **where** on Earth the feature is located
- Features = Shapes  + Location Data 
- The geometry of a tree can be the delineation of its crown ( Polygon )
- Of its stem,  (Polygon )
- or the point indicating its centre.  (Point )
-  A feature geometry is called **simple**  
 - when it consists of points connected by straight line pieces,  
 - and does not intersect itself.
]
.pull-right[

```{r,echo=FALSE, out.height="150px", out.width="450px"}

knitr::include_graphics("../../../materials/images/Holmes-Tree.jpg")

```

## So Finally, What is a Spatial Data Frame in R?
.pull-left[
- Features Geometries + **Attribute** data in a single Data Frame
- Geometries give **where** the feature is located **and** its shape
- **Attributes** describe other properties:  
    - Tree height (Quant)
    - Flower or foliage colour (Qual)
    - Trunk diameter at breast height at a particular date, (Quant)
    - Tree species and so on. (Qual)
]
.pull-right[
```{r, echo = FALSE,out.height="450px", out.width="900px"}

knitr::include_graphics("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/allisonhorst/stats-illustrations/master/rstats-artwork/sf.png")

```
]
---

## Kinds of Geospatial Geometries

.pull-left[

- Point/MultiPoint: buildings, offices, venues, etc in a city  
- LineString/MultiLineString: Roads, rivers and railways  
    
- Polygon: a lake, a golf course, or the border of a country  
  
- MultiPolygon: Any non-contiguous set of areas, a set of suburbs for example
]

.pull-right[


```{r,echo=FALSE, out.height="450px", out.width="900px"}

knitr::include_graphics("../../../materials/images/sf-classes.png")

```

]

## How are these shapes represented?


.pull-left[
![Geometry Primitives](https://cengel.github.io/R-spatial/img/wkt_primitives.png)
]

.pull-right[
![Multipart Geometry Representation](https://cengel.github.io/R-spatial/img/wkt_multipart.png)

]

- These formulaic descriptions are called **WKT: Well Known Text**  
- `lon` `lat` pairs. NOT separated by comma!
- Closed features have last point repeated
- Parentheses denotes shapes and nesting
- Note: Polygons can have **"holes"** in them!!

---

## Let us plot some hand-crafted simple geometries

---

## The `sf` : Spatial Data Frame: Point Geometry

.pull-left[

```{r plot1a, eval=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning = FALSE}

# Let's get the India Boundary
data("World")
india <- World %>% filter(iso_a3 == "IND")
crs_india <- st_crs(india)
points <- # Create 5 random points  #<<
  data.frame(lon = rnorm(5, 77, 2), #<<
             lat = rnorm(5, 23, 5)) #<<
points #<<

```
]

.pull-right[

```{r first-plot1a-out, ref.label='plot1a', echo=FALSE,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE,out.width ="90%",highlight.output = c(1:6)}

```
]

---
## The `sf` : Spatial Data Frame: Point Geometry

.pull-left[

```{r plot1b, eval=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning = FALSE}

# Let's get the India Boundary
data("world")
india <- World %>% filter(iso_a3 == "IND")
crs_india <- st_crs(india)
points <- # Create 5 random points
  data.frame(lon = rnorm(5, 77, 2),
             lat = rnorm(5, 23, 5))
# points
# Convert to spatial data frame
points_sf <- st_as_sf(points, 
         coords = c("lon", "lat"),
           crs = crs_india) 
points_sf #<<

```
]

.pull-right[

```{r first-plot1b-out, ref.label='plot1b', echo=FALSE,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE, out.width ="90%", highlight.output = c(2:11)}
```
]

## The `sf` : Spatial Data Frame: Point Geometry

.pull-left[

```{r plot1c, eval=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning = FALSE}

# Let's get the India Boundary
data("world")
india <- World %>% filter(iso_a3 == "IND")
crs_india <- st_crs(india)
points <- # Create 5 random points
  data.frame(lon = rnorm(5, 77, 2),
             lat = rnorm(5, 23, 5))
# points
# Convert to spatial data frame
points_sf <- st_as_sf(points,
         coords = c("lon", "lat"),
```

## The `sf`:Spatial Data Frame: Polygon Geometry

.pull-left[

```{r plot2a, eval=FALSE, message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}

# Let's create three SQUARES Using matrices)
# Center them over Central India (Lon: 77, Lat: 13)
outer <- matrix(c(0,0,10,0,10,10,0,10,0,0) + 
                  c(77,13), ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)
hole1 <- matrix(c(1,1,1,2,2,2,2,1,1,1) + 
                  c(77,13),ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)
hole2 <- matrix(c(5,5,5,6,6,6,6,5,5,5) + 
                  c(77,13),ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)
outer #<<
# Now pile all matrices into a **LIST*
pl1 <- list(outer = outer, hole1 = hole1, hole2 = hole2) #<<
str(pl1) #<<

```
]

.pull-right[

```{r first-plot2a-out, ref.label='plot2a', echo=FALSE,message=FALSE,warning=FALSE, out.width ="90%", highlight.output = c(2:6)}
```

]

## Why do we need Map Projections?

<iframe width="660" height="415" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/kIID5FDi2JQ" title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture" allowfullscreen></iframe>


---
## So, What is a Projection?

- A Process of taking a three-dimensional object and visualizing it on a two-dimensional surface
- No 100% perfect method for this
- Always introduces distortions
- Properties of projection methods: what they might preserve / distort

    - Shape ("Conformal" projection)
    - Area ("Equal Area" projection)
    - Angles ("Conformal" projection)
    - Distance ("Equidistant" projection)
    - Direction
    
- Projections are good at preserving only one or other of the above properties. 
- <u>[How to choose a Projection](http://www.geo.hunter.cuny.edu/~jochen/gtech201/lectures/lec6concepts/map%20coordinate%20systems/how%20to%20choose%20a%20projection.htm)</u>

# How do Projections Look on a Map?

---

```{r projections-1, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=7}

world <- ne_countries(returnclass = "sf")

world %>%
    st_transform("+proj=merc") %>%
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf() +
    # need to manually clip so Antarctica appears correct(ish)
    coord_sf(ylim = c(-2e07, NA)) +
    ggtitle("Mercator projection") + 
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

```

---
```{r projections-2, echo=FALSE,fig.height=4, fig.width=7}

world <- ne_countries(returnclass = "sf")
    world %>%
      st_transform("+proj=moll") %>%
      ggplot() +
      geom_sf() +
      ggtitle("Mollweide Projection") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

```
---

```{r projections-3, echo=FALSE,fig.height=4, fig.width=7}

library(patchwork)
world <- ne_countries(returnclass = "sf")
    world %>%
      st_transform("+proj=laea") %>%
      ggplot() +
      geom_sf() +
      ggtitle("Lambert Equal Area Projection") + 
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

```

---

```{r projections-4, echo=FALSE,fig.height=4, fig.width=7}

world <- ne_countries(returnclass = "sf")
    world %>%
      st_transform("+proj=cea") %>%
      ggplot() +
      geom_sf() +
      ggtitle("Equal area cylindrical AKA Gall_Peters Projection") + 
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

```
---

## Projections with `coord_sf()`


.pull-left[
Let's create an *Conical Equal Area* Projection in R. We can use the **Lambert Conical Equal-Area** Projection:

```{r csf, warning=FALSE, fig.show='hide', message=FALSE}

ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(data = world) + 
    geom_sf(data = india) + 
    geom_sf(data = points_sf, colour = "red", size = 2) + 
  coord_sf(crs = "+proj=laea +lat_0=23 +lon_0=77 +x_0=4321000 +y_0=3210000 +ellps=GRS80 +towgs84=0,0,0,0,0,0,0 +units=m +no_defs +type=crs") #<<

```
- <u>[Lambert Projection centered on India](https://grok.com/share/c2hhcmQtNA%3D%3D_97788889-ef95-41c2-9f16-278ec79f6907)</u>
- Uses the `proj` notation, which is (strangely?) deprecated in R!!
]

.pull-right[
```{r, echo=FALSE}

knitr::include_graphics(
  knitr::fig_chunk("csf", "png")
)

```
]

## To Summarize
- We obtain Spatial Data Frames from many sources, which we will see

- We very rarely create **small** Spatial Data by hand-coding WKT

- We can process with the Spatial Data with `dplyr` like verbs, (which we have not yet covered here)

Now we will: 
- Plot a variety of static and interactive maps
- Use Projections to show of the map in the right way
- We may need to *re-project* the data if needed
